title: Explore model-selectable visual grids for agent-centric pointing

body:
## Motivation

Agent Interface should not stop at exposing screenshots plus human-style pixel coordinates. The computer should remain universally operable through screenshots, keyboard and pointer input, but the observation/action representation can be made substantially more agent-friendly.

This issue collects a set of related research directions for **agent-native visual control**. It is intentionally a design/research issue rather than an implementation mandate. Astra/local research should decide which pieces are worth testing and in what order.

This complements:

- #2 — architecture risks / optimization backlog
- #3 — model-selectable visual grids
- #4 — north-star design thesis

## Working idea

Treat the interface less like a thin screenshot/mouse wrapper and more like a **stateful sensorimotor substrate**.

The model should be able to reference what it sees through stable, observation-bound visual addresses; request the form of feedback that is useful for the next action; and continue bounded manipulation only when the original authority remains valid.

The source GUI remains unchanged and universally accessible. These are optional representations and control contracts over that same GUI.

## 1. Visual Address instead of raw pixel coordinates alone

Current pointer operations ultimately target absolute screen coordinates. Keep that universal fallback, but explore a more explicit address form such as:

```text
VisualAddress {
    observation_id
    surface_id
    coordinate_frame_id
    selector
    offset
}
```

Possible selectors:

- absolute point;
- normalized surface-local point;
- grid cell + offset;
- ROI-local point;
- visual anchor + offset.

Every address should be bound to a specific observation/surface/frame so stale visual references can be rejected rather than silently reinterpreted.

Do not make X11 root coordinates part of the portable semantic contract merely because Linux/X11 is the current research backend.

## 2. Model-selectable Observation Presentation

Issue #3 proposes visual grids. Generalize that idea into a presentation choice rather than one permanent overlay.

Candidate presentations may include:

- raw frame;
- coarse grid;
- fine grid;
- ROI grid;
- high-resolution ROI;
- changed-region/delta emphasis;
- raw frame + compact change metadata.

The model may know when a plain screenshot is enough and when fine spatial assistance is useful.

A presentation request should not automatically require an extra remote planner round trip. Where possible, let the planner specify the desired next feedback presentation with the action/program that will produce it.

Preserve the unmodified source observation separately from any presentation transform.

## 3. Deterministic Visual Anchors

Current desktop pointer evidence shows that cursor displacement and application-level object displacement are not the same quantity. For example, a requested Inkscape cursor path can complete while the object moves less than requested.

Explore an optional deterministic visual anchor abstraction:

```text
VisualAnchor {
    anchor_id
    source_observation
    source_region
    deterministic_match/tracking description
}
```

The local runtime should not require a neural model. Candidate mechanisms can be simple and deterministic where suitable: template matching, color/edge regions, geometric features or other bounded local trackers.

Useful feedback could distinguish:

```text
cursor_delta
anchor_delta
anchor_confidence / lost
```

This gives the planner feedback about **application effect**, not merely input delivery.

## 4. Bounded visual servo / goal-directed manipulation

If visual anchors prove useful, consider a bounded local manipulation primitive that moves toward a planner-declared visual target while preserving the existing lease/authority safety model.

Conceptually:

```text
VisualServo {
    anchor
    target
    original lease/authority
    max_duration
    max_updates
    abort conditions
}
```

Possible abort conditions:

- focus/client/surface validity lost;
- geometry/frame invalidated;
- anchor lost;
- critical event retained;
- progress diverges;
- lease expires;
- cancellation.

This should remain deterministic local control, not a hidden local neural policy.

The planner chooses the target and policy bounds. The runtime only performs bounded observation/correction under those declared conditions.

## 5. Separate State and Event feedback

Consider making feedback semantics explicitly two-channel:

### State channel

Latest-useful, potentially lossy state:

- current/latest visual observation;
- changed regions;
- pointer state;
- current surface/context;
- anchor positions.

### Event channel

Retained/reliable semantic events:

- focus/client transition;
- lease expiry/cancel/release;
- modal/dialog appearance;
- anchor lost;
- critical warning;
- target reached;
- other subscribed conditions.

Latest-only state should never silently replace an event that must be acknowledged.

## 6. Make completion levels explicit

Keep input execution separate from semantic task effect. A useful shared vocabulary may be:

```text
INPUT_ACCEPTED
INPUT_EFFECT_OBSERVED
LOCAL_GOAL_REACHED
PROGRAM_TERMINAL
SEMANTIC_EFFECT_VERIFIED
TASK_SUCCEEDED
```

The Inkscape displacement evidence is a concrete reason: `pointer_drag completed` does not imply `object moved requested distance`.

Agent-facing feedback should prefer effect information when an independent or deterministic local measurement is available.

## 7. Planner-facing Continuation Ticket

The current owner work is developing owner identity/revision and same-hold continuation admission. A future planner-facing abstraction could expose that safely as a bounded continuation ticket, for example:

```text
ContinuationTicket {
    observation_id
    owner_id
    owner_revision
    original lease/authority
    surface/frame dependencies
    expires_at
    updates_remaining
}
```

A delayed or duplicate response must not revive released input or extend/rebind the original authority.

Continuation must be revalidated at admission against current owner state and observation dependencies. Historical input state attached to an image is evidence, not current permission.

Do not combine this with an unmodified preplanned tail that could later overwrite the correction. Explicit yield/path replacement semantics are required first.

## 8. Self-describing operation schema

The interface itself should be easy for a model to use correctly.

Expose machine-readable operation names, fields and limits so the planner does not have to infer details such as `modifier` versus another guessed field name.

This is part of agent-interface ergonomics, not merely documentation quality.

## Evaluation principles

Do not implement or promote all of these as one bundle by intuition.

For any candidate, predeclare the hypothesis and compare against a pinned baseline on fresh tasks. Useful metrics include:

- correctness hard gate;
- target / endpoint error;
- application-effect error, not only cursor error;
- number of corrective actions/observations;
- planner boundaries per successful task;
- time to useful feedback and semantic completion;
- observation/token cost when measurable;
- stale/wrong-target/release incidents;
- complexity and portability cost.

Use multiple domains: desktop, OpenTTD, continuous manipulation and later Mindustry/Luanti where appropriate.

## Design principle

The interface should not force a frontier model to imitate human hand-eye coordination when a deterministic agent-oriented representation offers more leverage.

At the same time, do not hide unresolved input semantics behind app-specific compensation or privileged engine actions.

A useful target is:

> Give the agent a better visual address space, better proprioceptive/effect feedback, and safe bounded continuation while preserving universal GUI compatibility and correctness.

This issue is a research menu. Astra should decide which ideas merit isolated experiments and may reject/defer any that do not move the correctness-preserving Pareto frontier.
title: Explore agent-native visual addressing and feedback contracts

body:
## Motivation

Issue #7 explores adaptive multi-view observation: overview, zoomed target ROI, destination ROI, changed region, grids, and temporal views. A practical concern is that sending each view as a separate image may increase model-visible context, vision-processing overhead, attention fragmentation, and latency.

A possible optimization is to **pack several logically separate views into one composite image** before presenting them to the frontier model.

Example:

```text
+----------------------+----------------------+
| A: overview          | B: target ROI 4x     |
|                      |                      |
|                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+
| C: destination ROI   | D: changed region    |
| 4x + grid            | / previous state     |
|                      |                      |
+----------------------+----------------------+
```

The hypothesis is not that one image is automatically cheaper than multiple images. Vision tokenization and preprocessing may depend on model/provider-specific resolution and tiling behavior. The question is empirical:

> Can one carefully packed composite preserve the useful information of multiple views while reducing total model-visible context cost, latency, or planner effort?

This is a presentation experiment, not a runtime semantic change or promotion request.

Related issues:

- #3 — model-selectable visual grids
- #5 — visual addressing and feedback contracts
- #7 — adaptive multi-view observation

## Candidate: Composite Observation View

Allow several derived views from one logical observation to be packed into one model-visible image.

Conceptually:

```text
CompositeView {
    source_observation
    canvas_size
    panels[]
}

Panel {
    panel_id
    source_frame
    source_rect
    destination_rect
    scale
    presentation_transform
}
```

Each panel must retain deterministic provenance and a mapping back to the original observation coordinate frame.

The composite is only a presentation transform. It must not become a new source of GUI truth.

## Candidate panel types

Useful combinations may include:

- overview + enlarged target;
- target + destination;
- overview + target + destination;
- target before + target after;
- raw ROI + grid-overlay ROI;
- overview + changed-region crop;
- multiple spatially distant ROIs that would otherwise require separate images.

Avoid packing panels merely because space is available. The goal is lower planner cost, not maximal visual density.

## Coordinate addressing

The planner should be able to refer to a panel without manually translating composite pixels back to screen coordinates.

Example:

```text
panel A = overview
panel B = target_roi
panel C = destination_roi

click(panel="B", x=.62, y=.41)
```

The runtime maps the panel-local normalized coordinate through the recorded source transform and then applies the ordinary stale-observation, surface, focus, authority and lease guards.

Do not let composite-canvas coordinates leak into the semantic GUI coordinate contract unless explicitly defined and validated.

## Important comparison arms

At minimum compare matched information presented as:

1. **Single plain overview**
2. **Several separate images**
3. **One composite image containing the same views**
4. **One composite image with only task-relevant views**

Where useful, add a fifth arm in which the planner explicitly requests the composite layout.

The experiment should hold source observations and semantic information as constant as possible. Otherwise it will be impossible to distinguish packing benefits from simply giving the model different information.

## Potential advantages

If supported by the target model/interface, composite packing may reduce:

- per-image framing/context overhead;
- number of separate visual objects the model must reconcile;
- repeated metadata describing each view;
- tool/result payload fragmentation;
- planner turns needed to inspect source and destination sequentially.

It may also make spatial comparison easier by placing related regions next to each other.

These are hypotheses, not established properties.

## Potential failure modes

Packing can also make performance worse:

- each panel becomes too small after fitting the canvas;
- resizing destroys small UI details;
- panel borders/labels consume useful pixels;
- the model confuses which panel is current or authoritative;
- duplicate representations of one object create ambiguity;
- visual attention is diluted by too many panels;
- a larger composite triggers equal or greater model-side image processing than separate images;
- packing increases local preparation latency without reducing planner work.

Therefore avoid assuming serialized bytes or image count predict model token cost.

## Layout should be deterministic and minimal

Start with simple layouts such as:

```text
2-up horizontal
2-up vertical
2x2 grid
large overview + one/two detail strips
```

Every panel should have an unambiguous short identifier (`A`, `B`, `C` or equivalent). Do not add decorative UI.

If labels are required, compare label/no-label variants because text rendered into images may itself consume visual capacity.

## Resolution allocation

A composite should not give every panel equal area by default.

For example:

```text
overview:     40% of pixels
target ROI:   30%
destination:  30%
```

or, for precision work:

```text
overview:     20%
target ROI:   40%
destination:  40%
```

Candidate allocation should be declared before matched runs. Adaptive allocation may be explored later, but avoid adding a hidden semantic selector during the first test.

## Temporal packing

A single image could also encode a short temporal comparison:

```text
A: before
B: current
C: delta-emphasis/current ROI
```

This may help the planner determine application effect in one model call without forwarding a frame sequence.

It must remain clear which image is newest, and historical panels must never be interpreted as current authority.

## Evaluation

Measure end-to-end effects, not image-file size alone.

For matched successful tasks record where available:

- correctness;
- task wall time;
- planner boundaries;
- model response latency;
- corrective actions / observations;
- time to first correct target selection;
- endpoint/application-effect error;
- number of model-visible images;
- actual model-visible image/token accounting where available;
- request/response payload bytes separately from token accounting;
- composite preparation time;
- failures caused by panel confusion or lost detail.

Useful questions include:

```text
3 separate images in 1 turn
vs
1 composite containing those 3 views
```

and:

```text
1 overview x multiple planner turns
vs
1 composite x fewer planner turns
```

A composite is useful only if the full end-to-end tradeoff improves while correctness is preserved.

## Scope / promotion rule

Keep plain screenshot presentation as the baseline.

Do not promote composite packing globally because one model/version happens to process it cheaply. Treat presentation efficiency as model- and interface-dependent evidence, and preserve a fallback to ordinary single-image observation.

If packing is beneficial only for precision manipulation or source/destination comparison, keep it as an optional presentation mode.

## Design principle

> Multiple useful visual perspectives do not necessarily need to be multiple model-visible images.

The Agent Interface may be able to perform cheap deterministic visual composition locally, giving the planner the same task-relevant evidence in a denser representation. Whether that actually saves context or time must be measured rather than assumed.
title: Explore composite visual packing to reduce multi-view context cost
